questions.question: Which fact supports the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem at the level of images?
options: The continuous image of a connected set is connected.
The image of every set under every function is finite.
The image of a disconnected set is always connected.
The image of a connected set under any function is always a singleton.
questions.explanation: The supporting fact is that the continuous image of a connected set is connected; since a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an interval, it contains every value between $f(\boldsymbol{a})$ and $f(\boldsymbol{b})$.
questions.source_support: A continuous image of a connected set is connected.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

A disconnected set can have a disconnected image; the identity on $\{0,1\}$ has image $\{0,1\}$, which is not connected.
The continuous image of a connected set is connected but need not be a single point; $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ has image $[0,1]$, and discontinuous functions are not covered by the theorem at all.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{E}$ be path-connected and $f:\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. If $f(\boldsymbol a)=1$ and $f(\boldsymbol b)=5$, why must some point have value $3$?
options: Because every path-connected set is finite.
Because $f$ must be linear on every path.
Because $3$ is the average of the coordinates of $\boldsymbol a$ and $\boldsymbol b$.
Compose $f$ with a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$ and apply the one-dimensional IVT.
questions.explanation: Path-connectedness gives a continuous path $\gamma$ from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$; then $f\circ\gamma$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ with values $1$ and $5$, so the one-dimensional IVT yields a point where it equals $3$.
questions.source_support: The relevant results mention proving the theorem on path-connected sets by composing with a path and using the one-dimensional IVT.

option_explanations: Path-connected sets need not be finite; $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself is path-connected and infinite. The argument instead uses a continuous path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ composed with $f$, applying the one-dimensional IVT to $f\circ\gamma$.
The argument uses continuity, not linearity; $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous and non-linear, and the IVT still applies along any path.
$3$ is the average of the values $1$ and $5$, and it lies between them; it has nothing to do with the coordinates of $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$.
